tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Add view transitions with an agent 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then prompt the agent with something like: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 Or prompt for a specific transition, such as: 32 33 - Morphing a thumbnail into a hero image 34 - Sliding between routes forward and back 35 - Crossfading content within the same route 36 37 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 38 39 ## Example 40 41 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 42 43 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 44 45 You can find the resources used in this example here: 46 47 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 48 - [Code](https://github.com/nextjs/react-view-transitions-demo) 49 50 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 66 67 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 68 69 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 70 71 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 72 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 73 import Image from 'next/image' 74 import Link from 'next/link' 75 76 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 77 return ( 78
79 {photos.map((photo) => ( 80 81 82 83 84 85 ))} 86
87 ) 88 } 89 ``` 90 91 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 92 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 93 import Image from 'next/image' 94 95 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 96 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 97 98 return ( 99 100
101 102
103 104 ) 105 } 106 ``` 107 108 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 217 218 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 219 220 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 221 222 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 332 333 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 334 335 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 336
337 {/* navigation links */} 338
339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. Let them pass through to the live page: 363 364 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 365 ::view-transition { 366 pointer-events: none; 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. I added view transitions using React's `<ViewTransition>` and the `Link` `transitionTypes` prop that come with this Next canary. It works in the App Router with no config change. Typecheck and `next build` both pass. There's no browser in this environment, though, so **I haven't watched any of the animations run**. Click through it in Chrome or Safari to confirm.

**Image morph** (`app/ProductGrid.tsx`, `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`)
- The grid thumbnail and the detail image are both wrapped in a `<ViewTransition>` with the same name (`product-image-${slug}`). React pairs them and animates size and position between the two pages, in both directions.
- The detail image sits outside the details `<Suspense>`, so it appears in the same render as the navigation. That's required for the morph; if it waited on a loading state, the two images wouldn't pair.
- I added CSS so the morph doesn't look stretched, since the thumbnail is 4:3 and the detail image is square. I also gave the thumbnail rounded top corners so its snapshot matches what you see on the card.

**Directional slides** (new `app/PageTransition.tsx`)
- Grid links slide forward and "← Back to products" slides back. Each page is wrapped in `PageTransition`, which slides the old content out and the new content in from the matching side.
- The wrapper goes in each `page.tsx`, not the layout, because the layout stays mounted between pages and would never animate.
- The browser's own back/forward buttons don't slide. Next doesn't tag those navigations with a direction, but the image morph still plays.

**Loading states**
- On both pages, the skeleton slides down and fades out quickly, then the content slides up and fades in.
- On the home page the grid isn't async, so its skeleton rarely shows. The animation is there for when it does.

**Reduced motion** (`app/globals.css`)
- With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, every view-transition animation runs instantly, so content just swaps.
- I also turned off the skeleton's pulsing animation in that mode, since you asked for all animations to respect the setting.

Clicks pass through the animation overlay, so the page stays clickable while a transition runs.

Browsers without the View Transitions API (it needs Chromium 125+ or a recent Safari or Firefox) still work but don't animate.

The build had added an extra path to `tsconfig.json` and created some build files; I reverted and removed those. I didn't touch your existing `package.json` change.
